skills.name: Logic
levels: I have seen puzzles where a rule tells me what must be true.
With a hint I can follow one rule and see what it forces.
I can follow a chain of rules on my own to find what must be true.
I can explain why the rule rules out the other choices.
I can teach the rule to someone else and spot it in a new puzzle.

skills.name: Deduction
levels: I have seen clues used to narrow down an answer.
With a hint I can cross off one thing a clue rules out.
I can cross off what it cannot be until one answer is left, on my own.
I can explain which clue ruled out each wrong answer.
I can teach someone to work through the clues in order and use it on a new set of clues.

skills.name: Patterns
levels: I have seen a row of shapes or numbers that follow a rule.
With a hint I can find what changes from one term to the next.
I can find the rule and predict the next term on my own.
I can explain why the rule keeps working further down the list.
I can teach the rule and use it to predict a pattern I have not seen before.

skills.name: Spatial reasoning
levels: I have seen shapes that fold, rotate or fit together.
With a hint I can picture one shape turned or flipped.
I can picture a shape moved or combined on my own to solve the puzzle.
I can explain why a shape fits or does not fit in a space.
I can teach the trick and use it on a shape I have not tried before.

skills.name: Proof
levels: I have seen someone show that an answer must always be true.
With a hint I can check that a claim works for one example.
I can build an argument that shows a claim is always true, on my own.
I can explain why checking a few examples is not enough.
I can teach my proof to someone and use the same method on a new claim.

skills.name: Algorithms
levels: I have seen a set of steps used to solve a problem every time.
With a hint I can follow the steps in order on paper.
I can follow a set of steps to the answer on my own.
I can explain why the steps always land on the right answer.
I can teach the steps and use them on a problem the steps were not written for.

skills.name: Number sense
levels: I have seen a fast estimate made without a calculator.
With a hint I can round numbers to make an estimate.
I can estimate an answer in my head on my own before I check it.
I can explain why my estimate is close and where the gap comes from.
I can teach a rounding trick and use it on a new kind of question.

skills.name: Money
levels: I have seen prices, change and totals worked out.
With a hint I can add up a total or work out change.
I can work out a total, change or a better deal on my own.
I can explain why one price is a better deal than another.
I can teach how to compare deals and use it on a real receipt.

skills.name: Fractions
levels: I have seen fractions with different bottoms added together.
With a hint I can make two bottoms match before I add.
I can add or subtract fractions with different bottoms on my own.
I can explain why the bottoms have to match before I add.
I can teach the common bottom trick and use it on a fraction I have not seen.

skills.name: Decimals
levels: I have seen a decimal point move when a number is multiplied or divided.
With a hint I can move the point the right number of places.
I can multiply or divide decimals on my own by moving the point.
I can explain why moving the point works the way it does.
I can teach the point trick and use it on money or measurements.

skills.name: Percent
levels: I have seen a percent turned into a fraction of one hundred.
With a hint I can turn a percent into a fraction or decimal.
I can work out a percent of a number on my own.
I can explain why percent means out of one hundred.
I can teach percent and use it on a discount or a score.

skills.name: Ratios
levels: I have seen two amounts compared as a ratio.
With a hint I can scale a ratio up or down.
I can compare or scale a ratio on my own.
I can explain why scaling both sides the same way keeps the ratio fair.
I can teach ratios and use them on a recipe or a map.

skills.name: Negative numbers
levels: I have seen numbers below zero on a number line.
With a hint I can find a negative number on the line.
I can add and subtract with negative numbers on my own.
I can explain why subtracting a negative moves the other way.
I can teach negative numbers and use them on a temperature or a score.

skills.name: Equations
levels: I have seen a letter stand for a missing number in an equation.
With a hint I can do the same thing to both sides of an equation.
I can solve an equation for the missing number on my own.
I can explain why the same move on both sides keeps it balanced.
I can teach equations and use them on a problem written in words.

skills.name: Exponents
levels: I have seen a number multiplied by itself again and again, written as a power.
With a hint I can turn a small power into its multiplication chain.
I can work out powers and use them inside expressions on my own.
I can explain why an exponent is not the same as multiplying once.
I can teach exponents and spot a repeated-multiplication count in a problem I have not seen.

skills.name: Coordinates
levels: I have seen a point named by how far across and how far up it sits.
With a hint I can plot a point from its (x, y) pair.
I can plot and read points in all four quadrants on my own.
I can explain why the order of the two numbers in a pair matters.
I can teach coordinates and use them to place a shape I have not plotted before.

skills.name: Blocks
levels: I have seen a program built by snapping blocks together.
With a hint I can snap the right block into a program.
I can build a short program out of blocks on my own.
I can explain what each block in my program does.
I can teach block coding and use it to build something new.

skills.name: Sensors
levels: I have seen a sensor read light, motion or touch.
With a hint I can read one sensor value on the screen.
I can read a sensor and use its value in a program on my own.
I can explain why the sensor reading changes when the world changes.
I can teach sensors and use one I have not used before.

skills.name: Loops
levels: I have seen a block of code repeat itself.
With a hint I can set a loop to repeat a set number of times.
I can write a loop that repeats or repeats until something happens, on my own.
I can explain why a loop saves me from writing the same block over and over.
I can teach loops and use one to solve a new kind of repeating task.

skills.name: Conditionals
levels: I have seen a program do one thing or another depending on a check.
With a hint I can fill in an if block with the right check.
I can write an if or if-else block on my own.
I can explain why the program only runs one branch, not both.
I can teach conditionals and use them to make a new decision in a program.

skills.name: Variables
levels: I have seen a program store a number in a named box.
With a hint I can set a variable to a starting value.
I can create and update a variable on my own.
I can explain why the variable changes as the program runs.
I can teach variables and use one to keep score in a new program.

skills.name: Functions
levels: I have seen a group of steps packed into one named block.
With a hint I can call a function that already exists.
I can write my own function and call it on my own.
I can explain why packing steps into a function saves repeating them.
I can teach functions and use one to organise a program I have not written before.

skills.name: Debugging
levels: I have seen a program fixed after it did the wrong thing.
With a hint I can find the one block that is not doing what I expect.
I can test my program step by step and find the bug on my own.
I can explain why that block caused the wrong behaviour.
I can teach a debugging habit and use it on a program I did not write.

skills.name: Python
levels: I have seen code typed as text instead of blocks.
With a hint I can type a short line of Python and run it.
I can write a short Python program on my own.
I can explain why my Python code does the same thing as the blocks.
I can teach a Python line and use it in a new program.

skills.name: Data
levels: I have seen numbers collected from a sensor over time.
With a hint I can read one value out of a list of collected data.
I can collect and look through a set of data on my own.
I can explain what the data shows about what happened.
I can teach data collection and use it to answer a question I have not asked before.

skills.name: AI basics
levels: I have seen a program that learned from examples instead of being told exact rules.
With a hint I can point out what examples a model was trained on.
I can check what a model got right and wrong on my own.
I can explain why a model only knows what it was shown.
I can teach how a model learns and use that idea to judge a new model.

skills.name: Circuits
levels: I have seen a circuit make one loop from the battery through parts and back.
With a hint I can wire a simple loop that lights an LED.
I can build a circuit from my own drawing and test it before powering it, on my own.
I can explain why current flows in my circuit and what each part in the loop is doing.
I can teach a circuit to someone else and design a new one that answers a new question.

skills.name: Voice
levels: I have seen a speaker use a strong, clear voice.
With a hint I can slow down and speak louder for the room.
I can use pace, volume and pauses on my own when I talk.
I can explain which part of my voice made a point land.
I can teach voice tricks and use them in a talk I have not given before.

skills.name: Structure
levels: I have seen a talk that has a clear beginning, middle and end.
With a hint I can put my points in an order that makes sense.
I can structure a talk with an opening, points and a close, on my own.
I can explain why that order made the talk easier to follow.
I can teach a talk structure and use it on a new topic.

skills.name: Claim, reason, example
levels: I have seen a point backed up with a reason and an example.
With a hint I can add a reason to a claim I make.
I can make a claim, give a reason and back it with an example, on my own.
I can explain why an example makes a claim more convincing.
I can teach claim, reason, example and use it in a debate I have not prepared.

skills.name: Steelmanning
levels: I have seen someone state the other side's best argument before answering it.
With a hint I can say the strongest version of the other side's point.
I can steelman the other side before I argue against it, on my own.
I can explain why steelmanning makes my own argument stronger.
I can teach steelmanning and use it on a side I disagree with.

skills.name: Cross-examination
levels: I have seen someone ask a question that finds a weak spot in an argument.
With a hint I can ask one question about a claim I am not sure of.
I can ask questions that test another argument on my own.
I can explain why my question exposed a weak spot.
I can teach cross-examination and use it in a debate on a new motion.

skills.name: Listening
levels: I have seen someone repeat back what another person said before replying.
With a hint I can repeat back the other side's point in my own words.
I can listen for the other side's real point and respond to it, on my own.
I can explain what I heard that changed how I replied.
I can teach active listening and use it in a conversation that is not a debate.

skills.name: Reflection
levels: I have seen someone look back at a talk and say what they would change.
With a hint I can name one thing I would do differently next time.
I can reflect on my own talk and name what worked and what did not, on my own.
I can explain why that change would make the next talk better.
I can teach reflection and use it after a talk on a topic I have not given before.

skills.name: Analogy
levels: I have seen a tricky idea explained with a picture from everyday life.
With a hint I can match an idea to an everyday thing that works like it.
I can explain an idea with my own analogy on my own.
I can explain where my analogy fits the idea and where it stops fitting.
I can teach an idea with an analogy and build a new one for an idea I have just met.

skills.name: Patterns
levels: I have seen a row where something repeats.
With a hint I can point to what comes next.
I can tap what comes next in a pattern on my own.
I can say why that one comes next.
I can make my own pattern for someone else to finish.

skills.name: Sorting
levels: I have seen things put into groups that match.
With a hint I can put one thing into the right group.
I can sort a set of things into groups on my own.
I can say what makes each group the same.
I can sort a new set of things nobody showed me how to sort.

skills.name: Sequencing
levels: I have seen steps put in the order they happen.
With a hint I can put two steps in the right order.
I can put a set of steps in order on my own.
I can say why that step has to come first.
I can put a new set of steps in order without help.

skills.name: Matching
levels: I have seen two things that go together.
With a hint I can find one match.
I can match things that go together on my own.
I can say why two things match.
I can find a match nobody pointed out to me.

skills.name: Spatial
levels: I have seen shapes that fit inside or next to each other.
With a hint I can turn a shape to see if it fits.
I can fit shapes together on my own.
I can say why a shape fits in one spot and not another.
I can build something new out of shapes that fit together.

skills.name: Counting
levels: I have seen things counted one at a time.
With a hint I can count up to a small number.
I can count a group of things on my own.
I can say how many are left after some are taken away.
I can count a group nobody has shown me how to count before.

skills.name: Comparing
levels: I have seen two piles where one has more than the other.
With a hint I can point to the pile with more.
I can pick the pile with more on my own and count to check.
I can say how counting shows which pile has more.
I can compare two piles nobody has shown me and say which has more.

skills.name: Sounds
levels: I have heard words that start with the same sound.
With a hint I can say the first sound of my own name.
I can pick the picture that starts with a sound on my own.
I can tell when two words start with the same sound.
I can find a new word that starts with a sound all by myself.

skills.name: Soldering
levels: I have seen a solder joint made and can say what a good one looks like.
With the adult beside me I can make a clean practice joint on scrap.
I can solder a small circuit from my own plan, joint by joint, keeping every bench rule, with the adult watching but not helping.
I can explain why the joint gets heated before the solder touches it, and spot a cold joint by eye.
I can teach someone their first joint and repair a bad joint I find with the right fix.

skills.name: Inequalities
levels: I have seen a bigger-than sentence as a balance that stays tipped to one side.
With a hint I can test whether a number makes an inequality true.
I can find which whole numbers make a one-step inequality true, and draw them on a number line, on my own.
I can explain why the balance point itself is in or out, and what the filled or hollow circle says.
I can teach inequalities and read a shaded number line back into words for a problem I have not seen.

skills.name: Primes and factors
levels: I have seen a number split into factors and heard why some numbers are called prime.
With a hint I can hunt a number's factors in pairs or grow its factor tree.
I can find all factors of a number, run the sieve on a hundred chart, and break a number into prime leaves, on my own.
I can explain why 1 is not prime and why the pair hunt can stop when the pairs meet in the middle.
I can teach the sieve and use factor pairs or prime atoms to crack a number puzzle I have not seen.

skills.name: Statistics
levels: I have seen a list of readings squeezed into one number, like the mean.
With a hint I can find the mean, median or range of a small list.
I can compute mean, median and range of my own data and say what each one tells.
I can explain why a wild reading drags the mean but not the median, and pick the fairer number for the job.
I can teach mean, median and range, and use them to defend a decision made from my own data.

skills.name: Gcd and lcm
levels: I have seen two numbers share a biggest piece and meet at a first common multiple.
With a hint I can find the gcd or lcm of two small numbers by listing.
I can find a gcd with the subtraction game and an lcm by counting to the first meeting, on my own.
I can explain why subtracting the smaller number never loses the piece the two numbers share.
I can teach gcd and lcm, and spot where a new puzzle secretly asks for one of them.

skills.name: Asking machines well
levels: I have seen the same question asked badly and well, with two different answers back.
With a hint I can name the job, the facts and the limits before I ask.
I can write an ask with job, facts and limits on my own, and compare what comes back.
I can explain what the machine had to guess when my ask left facts out, and check its answer against something I can test.
I can teach someone to brief a machine well, and spot which part a weak ask is missing.

skills.name: Clock math
levels: I have seen counting wrap around a loop, like clock hours starting over after 12.
With a hint I can find where a count lands after it wraps, by throwing away full loops.
I can use remainders to answer wrap-around questions about clocks, weekdays and codes on my own.
I can explain why full loops change nothing and only the remainder decides where you land.
I can teach clock math and spot a hidden loop in a problem that never mentions a clock.

skills.name: Dependent and independent variables
levels: I have seen an experiment where one quantity changes because another one does.
With a hint I can point at which quantity is doing the driving and which one answers to it.
I can name the independent and dependent variable in an experiment or on a graph on my own.
I can explain why the dependence runs one way only, and what a flat or steep line says about it.
I can teach the idea and choose sensible variables for an experiment I design myself.

skills.name: Rhyming
levels: I have heard two words whose endings sound the same.
With a hint I can tell when two words rhyme.
I can tap the picture whose name rhymes on my own.
I can say my own word that rhymes with one I hear.
I can make up a silly rhyme nobody taught me.

skills.name: Angles
levels: I have seen angles measured in degrees and can point out a square corner, a straight line and a full turn.
With a hint I can measure an angle with the protractor and draw an angle I am asked for.
I can find a missing angle on a straight line, in a triangle or in a four-sided shape, on my own.
I can explain why every triangle's torn corners line up into a straight line, and why estimating first keeps the protractor's two scales from fooling me.
I can teach the torn-corners discovery and use angle sums to find a missing corner in a shape I have not seen before.

skills.name: Counting ways
levels: I have seen the ways counted by multiplying: each new choice multiplies what came before.
With a hint I can count the ways for two or three stacked choices, like the rings of a code lock.
I can count codes, menus and light patterns by multiplying choices, and spot when a count explodes into the millions, on my own.
I can explain why free-standing choices multiply while tangled choices need the ways added spot by spot.
I can teach the multiplication principle and pick the right counting move for a puzzle I have not seen before.

skills.name: Design and planning
levels: I have seen a build planned before it was built: sketches first, then a plan, then parts.
With help I can sketch more than one idea for a problem and say what each would do for its person.
I can pick an idea with reasons, draw a labeled plan with real sizes, and list every part it needs, on my own.
I can explain why the scariest part of a plan needs a plan B before the first part is bought.
I can plan a build for someone else, price it against a cap, and change the plan honestly when the world pushes back.

skills.name: Area and surface area
levels: I have seen an odd shape's area found by chopping it into rectangles.
With a hint I can find the area of an L shape, a right triangle or a parallelogram by chopping, halving or sliding.
I can find areas by decomposition, draw a multiplication as a split rectangle, and total a box's six faces from its net, on my own.
I can explain why moving a cut piece never changes the area, and why the split rectangle is the distributive property drawn.
I can teach the chopping tricks and find the area or surface area of a shape I have never met.

skills.name: Probability
levels: I have seen chance written as a count: the ways you want out of all the ways there are.
With a hint I can list all the ways a small experiment can land and count the ones I want.
I can count outcomes with the multiplication principle, turn the count into a chance, and say what the long run promises, on my own.
I can explain why a short run wobbles off the promise, and why dice never remember and never owe.
I can teach chance as counting and spot a wrong claim about luck when I hear one.

skills.name: Pythagoras
levels: I have seen the two small squares on a right triangle's legs cut up to exactly fill the square on its longest side.
With a hint I can add the two leg squares and hunt the number that squares to the total.
I can find a right triangle's longest side, or the exact distance between two plotted points, on my own.
I can explain why the cut up pieces must fill the big square exactly, with nothing missing and nothing left over.
I can teach the square on the side and use it to measure a distance nobody drew a triangle for.

skills.name: Volume
levels: I have seen a box's volume counted by filling it with little cubes.
With a hint I can multiply a box's three edges to get its volume.
I can find the volume of a box on my own, even when its edges are fractions.
I can explain why edge times edge times edge counts cubes, and why a fractional edge just means counting in smaller cubes.
I can teach volume and use it on a container nobody has measured for me.

skills.name: Version control
levels: I have seen work saved as a camp you can walk back to.
With a hint I can start a repo, add a file and make a commit.
I can commit my work at sensible save points on my own.
I can explain what add does that commit does not, and why walking back is safe.
I can teach someone to start a repo and restore a file from an earlier camp.

skills.name: Rebuttal and the flow
levels: I have seen someone answer an argument point by point instead of starting a new speech.
With a hint I can write the other side's points in a column while they are still talking.
I can flow a speech and answer the points I chose, on my own.
I can explain why answering what was said beats answering what I expected to hear.
I can teach the flow to someone else and use it on a motion I have never argued before.

skills.name: Writing it down for the next person
levels: I have seen instructions that tell someone else how to run a program.
With a hint I can write down the steps I took so someone could repeat them.
I can write instructions that a person who was not there can follow on their own.
I can explain why a step that is obvious to me still has to be written down.
I can teach someone to write for a stranger, and fix my own page by watching one person stall.

skills.name: Evidence
levels: I have heard the difference between someone saying what they think and someone showing what they measured.
With a hint I can add a real number to a point I have already made.
I can build a point that carries its own evidence, and say where the evidence came from, on my own.
I can explain why a number I cannot name the source of is worth less than no number at all.
I can teach someone else to test their own points by asking how do I know that, and to drop the ones that fail.

skills.name: The summary speech
levels: I have seen a last speech pick one argument instead of repeating the whole round faster.
With a hint I can choose one point off my flow and spend a whole minute on it.
I can write and deliver a summary that names what I am dropping and why, on my own.
I can explain why the point I am winning beats the point I like best, and show the row on the flow that proves it.
I can teach someone else to collapse to their best point, and do it on a motion I have never argued before.

skills.name: Lines and slope
levels: I have seen a line described by how much it climbs for each step across.
With a hint I can work out the slope from two points a line passes through.
I can write the law of a line from a table of my own numbers, on my own.
I can explain what the slope and the starting amount each mean in the real thing the line is about.
I can teach slope to someone else and use the law of a line on a problem written in words.

skills.name: C++
levels: I have seen a program translated before it runs instead of read one line at a time.
With a hint I can compile and run a short C++ program.
I can write, compile and fix a short C++ program on my own.
I can explain what the compiler checks before anything runs, and why that helps me.
I can teach a C++ line to someone else and rewrite a program of mine in it.

skills.name: Judging and the RFD
levels: I have seen a judge give a reason for a decision instead of only a result.
With a hint I can fill in a ballot while a round is still playing.
I can name the clash, weigh it and announce a verdict on my own.
I can explain why a side I agreed with can still lose the round they argued.
I can teach someone else to judge and give an RFD on a motion I have never argued.

skills.name: Coaching
levels: I have seen someone help a debater get ready instead of debating themselves.
With a hint I can ask my debater a question that makes their point stronger.
I can build a case file with somebody, in their words, without writing their speech for them.
I can explain why the two hardest questions have to be met in a drill before they arrive in a round.
I can teach the signposting I use to someone else and pick the two things worth saying between speeches.

skills.name: Producing an event
levels: I have been in a show that somebody else planned and run.
With a hint I can put the parts of an event in a sensible order.
I can write a run of show with minutes beside every segment and add them up.
I can explain why a segment that needs one particular guest is a segment that has to be redesigned.
I can produce an event end to end: decide what it is for, give every person a job or tell them they have none, and run it on the day.

skills.name: Physics
levels: I have seen a real number come from a real measurement, like a voltage, a distance, or a time.
With a hint I can predict a number before I measure it, and check how close I was.
I can pick the right tool, a multimeter, a ruler, a stopwatch, or a camera, and measure a real physical quantity on my own.
I can explain why my measurement came out the way it did, using the physics idea behind it.
I can teach the idea to someone else and design my own measurement to test a new question.

skills.name: Practice craft
levels: I have seen a hard bar get easier by being practised on its own, slowly.
With a hint I can pick the hard bars of a piece and practise them before anything else.
I can plan a sitting on my own: hard bars first, slow, then once through.
I can explain why slow, small, repeated practice teaches fingers faster than playing the whole piece.
I can teach someone how to practise a piece they are stuck on.

skills.name: Listening back
levels: I have heard a recording of my own playing and noticed one thing I did not hear while playing.
With a hint I can name one thing to fix after listening back.
I can record a sitting, listen, and pick the one thing to fix next, on my own.
I can explain why I cannot hear my own slips while I am busy playing.
I can listen to someone else play and give them one useful thing to fix.

skills.name: Steady pulse
levels: I have played along with a metronome or a steady clap.
With a hint I can find the beat of a piece and count it out loud.
I can keep a steady pulse through a whole piece, even through the hard bars.
I can explain why slowing down in a hard bar is a rhythm slip, not a note slip.
I can help someone keep a steady beat while they play.

skills.name: Reading the notes
levels: I have read a short new line of music without being shown it first.
With a hint I can work out a new bar from the page: the notes, the rhythm, the fingers.
I can sight-read a short new piece slowly, on my own, and keep going through mistakes.
I can explain what I look at first on a new page, and why.
I can teach someone how to read a bar they have never seen.

skills.name: The map of the piece
levels: I have noticed that a piece has parts that come back.
With a hint I can draw the map of a piece: its sections and where they repeat.
I can play a piece from memory using its map, starting from any section.
I can explain why knowing the map makes a piece easier to remember than the notes alone.
I can help someone find the map of a piece they are learning.

skills.name: Playing for people
levels: I have played a piece for someone else, start to finish.
With a hint I can keep going after a slip instead of starting again.
I can perform a piece for the family, say its name, keep going through slips, and finish.
I can explain what nerves do to my playing and what I do about it.
I can help someone get ready to play for people.

skills.name: Levers, gears and torque
levels: I have seen a lever or a gear make a push bigger or faster, and felt the trade.
With a hint I can predict which way a gear pair trades speed for force, and by how much.
I can measure a force with a spring scale, work out a ratio, and choose a gear or lever for a job on my own.
I can explain why a machine cannot give more work out than goes in, only trade force for distance.
I can design a mechanism for someone else's job and say what it will trade away.

skills.name: Structures and loads
levels: I have seen a triangle hold its shape where a square leaned.
With a hint I can find the member of a structure that carries the load and the one that is idle.
I can build a structure to a target load, test it to failure, and say where and why it broke.
I can explain why things break where pieces meet and how to design the joint for it.
I can help someone strengthen a structure without adding much material.

skills.name: Design and 3D printing
levels: I have measured a real part with calipers and seen how far a print came out from the drawing.
With a hint I can model a simple part in a CAD tool with the right dimensions.
I can design, print, measure and fix a part that fits a real thing, on my own.
I can explain tolerance, why a hole prints smaller than drawn, and how infill trades strength for time.
I can design a part for someone else's machine from their sketch and their numbers.

skills.name: Circuits as a system
levels: I have read a schematic and found the same circuit on the breadboard.
With a hint I can draw a schematic of a circuit I built and read one number from a datasheet.
I can measure current and voltage where they matter, pick a resistor from the numbers, and draw the schematic on my own.
I can explain why a motor needs a driver and what a datasheet's limits protect.
I can help someone turn a breadboard into a schematic they could send to be made.

skills.name: Measuring and testing
levels: I have made the same measurement three times and seen it wobble.
With a hint I can plan a test: what to change, what to keep the same, what to measure.
I can run a fair test, log it in a table, chart it, and say what the numbers do and do not show, on my own.
I can explain why one run is not a verdict and how many runs are enough for a claim.
I can design a test for someone else's claim and say what result would prove them wrong.

skills.name: The engineer's notebook
levels: I have written down a number from a test and what I changed after it.
With a hint I can keep a log another person could follow: what I did, what happened, what next.
I can keep a Maker's Log through a build with the numbers, the failures and the fixes in order, on my own.
I can explain why an engineer writes the failure down first and the fix second.
I can hand my notebook to someone and they can rebuild what I built.

skills.name: Chess tactics
levels: I have seen a fork, a pin or a back-rank mate on a board.
With a hint I can find the one move that wins a piece or gives mate in a puzzle.
I can find the tactic in a puzzle on my own, name it, and check that the move is safe.
I can explain why the tactic works and what the defender should have done a move earlier.
I can set a tactics puzzle for someone else and check their answer.

skills.name: Place value
levels: I have seen numbers where a digit means something different depending on where it sits.
With a hint I can read the value of one digit in a big number.
I can read, write and compare big numbers by their digits on my own.
I can explain why moving a digit one place changes its value by ten times.
I can teach place value and use it to compare numbers I have not seen before.

skills.name: Multiplication
levels: I have seen multiplication facts used to count groups fast.
With a hint I can work out one multiplication fact I do not know by heart.
I can recall my multiplication facts and use them on my own.
I can explain why a fact I do not remember can be built from ones I do.
I can teach multiplication facts and use them instantly inside a harder problem.

skills.name: Division
levels: I have seen division used to split a number into equal groups.
With a hint I can divide a number and find what is left over.
I can divide multi-digit numbers on my own, remainder and all.
I can explain what a remainder means for the numbers in the problem.
I can teach long division and use it inside a bigger problem.

skills.name: Order of operations
levels: I have seen a calculation with more than one operation in it.
With a hint I can find which part of the calculation to do first.
I can work through a mixed calculation in the right order on my own.
I can explain why doing the operations in a different order changes the answer.
I can teach the order of operations and use it on a calculation with brackets and powers.

skills.name: Estimation
levels: I have seen a number rounded to make a calculation easier.
With a hint I can round one number to check if an answer looks right.
I can round and estimate an answer before I calculate, on my own.
I can explain why my estimate should land close to the exact answer.
I can teach estimation and use it to catch a mistake in someone else's answer.

skills.name: Measurement
levels: I have seen units used to measure length, weight, time or capacity.
With a hint I can convert one measurement into a different unit.
I can convert between units and use them in a calculation on my own.
I can explain why the number changes but the amount does not when I convert.
I can teach unit conversion and use it inside a real measuring problem.

skills.name: Word problems
levels: I have seen a word problem that needs more than one step to solve.
With a hint I can find the first step hiding inside a word problem.
I can break a word problem into steps and solve it on my own.
I can explain why I chose that order of steps and not another.
I can teach how to plan a multi-step word problem and use it on a new one.

skills.name: Square roots
levels: I have seen a square root used to undo a squared number.
With a hint I can find the square root of a perfect square.
I can find and estimate square roots on my own.
I can explain why a square root and squaring undo each other.
I can teach square roots and use them inside a harder problem.

skills.name: Expressions and the distributive law
levels: I have seen a bracket multiplied out across a sum inside it.
With a hint I can multiply out one bracket or combine matching terms.
I can simplify an expression with the distributive law on my own.
I can explain why multiplying out a bracket keeps the value the same.
I can teach the distributive law and use it to simplify an expression I have not seen before.

skills.name: Systems of equations
levels: I have seen two equations share the same x and y, and their graphs cross at one point.
With a hint I can check whether a point satisfies both equations at once.
I can solve two equations together by substitution or elimination on my own.
I can explain why the crossing point is the only pair that fits both lines.
I can teach systems of equations and set one up from a problem written in words.

skills.name: Polynomials
levels: I have seen terms with different powers of the same letter added together in one expression.
With a hint I can combine the like terms in a polynomial.
I can add, subtract and multiply polynomials on my own.
I can explain why only matching powers can be combined.
I can teach polynomials and multiply two brackets I have not seen before.

skills.name: Factoring
levels: I have seen a polynomial written as a product of simpler pieces instead of a sum.
With a hint I can pull a shared factor out of every term.
I can factor a trinomial or a special pattern on my own.
I can explain why factoring undoes multiplying out brackets.
I can teach factoring and pick the right pattern for a polynomial I have not seen.

skills.name: Quadratics
levels: I have seen an equation with a squared letter make a curved graph called a parabola.
With a hint I can solve a quadratic equation once it is already factored.
I can solve and graph a quadratic on my own, by factoring or the formula.
I can explain why a quadratic can have two answers, one answer or none.
I can teach quadratics and choose the fastest method for one I have not seen.

skills.name: Functions
levels: I have seen a rule that pairs every input with exactly one output.
With a hint I can check whether a table or graph is a function.
I can evaluate a function and find its domain and range on my own.
I can explain why a function can only give one output for each input.
I can teach functions and read one straight off a graph I have not seen.

skills.name: Absolute value
levels: I have seen absolute value measure how far a number sits from zero.
With a hint I can split an absolute value equation into its two cases.
I can solve absolute value equations and inequalities on my own.
I can explain why an absolute value equation can have two answers.
I can teach absolute value as distance and use it on a problem I have not seen.

skills.name: Exponential growth
levels: I have seen an amount double or halve again and again instead of adding the same amount each time.
With a hint I can find the next step of a doubling or halving pattern.
I can write and use an exponential pattern from a percent growth rate on my own.
I can explain why repeated multiplying grows faster than repeated adding, given enough steps.
I can teach exponential patterns and spot one hiding in a situation described in words.

skills.name: Scientific notation
levels: I have seen a very large or very small number written as one digit times a power of ten.
With a hint I can move the decimal point to write a number in scientific notation.
I can convert numbers into and out of scientific notation on my own.
I can explain why the power of ten counts how many places the point moved.
I can teach scientific notation and use it to compare numbers of very different sizes.

skills.name: Permutations and combinations
levels: I have seen order matter for some counts and not matter for others.
With a hint I can tell whether a counting problem cares about order.
I can count arrangements and selections with permutations and combinations on my own.
I can explain why dividing by the repeats turns an arrangement count into a selection count.
I can teach permutations and combinations and pick the right one for a count I have not seen.

skills.name: Proof
levels: I have seen a two-column proof line up a claim with the reason that backs it.
With a hint I can write the converse of a true statement and test it with a counterexample.
I can write a two-column proof in the right order, on my own.
I can explain why one counterexample is enough to break a claim, but no number of examples proves it.
I can teach the shape of a proof and use it to argue a new claim about angles or triangles.

skills.name: Congruence
levels: I have seen two triangles matched up corner by corner to check they are exactly the same shape and size.
With a hint I can pick SSS, SAS, ASA or AAS to show two triangles are congruent.
I can prove two triangles congruent and use CPCTC to prove a fact about their matching parts, on my own.
I can explain why SSA is not a real test, even though three matching parts sound like enough.
I can teach the congruence tests and use them on a pair of overlapping triangles nobody drew apart.

skills.name: Similarity
levels: I have seen a small triangle and a big triangle with the same angles, just stretched.
With a hint I can use AA to show two triangles are similar and set up a ratio for a missing side.
I can prove two triangles similar and use the scale factor to find a side, a perimeter or an area, on my own.
I can explain why a triangle's area grows by the scale factor squared, not by the scale factor itself.
I can teach similarity and use it for an indirect measurement, like a tree's height from its shadow.

skills.name: Circles
levels: I have seen a circle's central angle match the arc it cuts off exactly.
With a hint I can find an arc, a chord or an inscribed angle from the pieces I am given.
I can find an angle or a length where chords, secants and tangents meet a circle, on my own.
I can explain why an inscribed angle is always half its arc, no matter where its vertex sits.
I can teach the circle rules and use them on a diagram with chords, secants and tangents all at once.

skills.name: Trigonometry
levels: I have seen a right triangle's sides named opposite, adjacent and hypotenuse from one of its angles.
With a hint I can use sine, cosine or tangent to find a missing side of a right triangle.
I can set up and solve an angle of elevation or depression problem with the right ratio, on my own.
I can explain why the same ratio gives a different answer once the angle it is measured from changes.
I can teach the three ratios and use them on a real distance nobody drew a triangle around.

skills.name: Transformations
levels: I have seen a shape slide, flip or turn on the coordinate plane without changing its size.
With a hint I can write the coordinate rule for a translation, reflection or rotation.
I can apply a translation, reflection, rotation or dilation to a figure's coordinates, on my own.
I can explain why a dilation changes a figure's size but a translation, reflection or rotation never does.
I can teach transformations and use two of them together, or find a figure's lines of symmetry.

skills.name: Surface area
levels: I have seen a solid's net unfolded flat so every face can be seen and measured at once.
With a hint I can total a prism's or cylinder's faces from its net to find its surface area.
I can find the surface area of a prism, cylinder, pyramid, cone or sphere, on my own.
I can explain why a cone's curved surface is a sector, and why a sphere has no flat net at all.
I can teach surface area and use it on a solid built from more than one shape.

skills.name: Polygons
levels: I have seen a polygon cut into triangles from one corner to find its angle sum.
With a hint I can find a polygon's interior or exterior angle sum from its number of sides.
I can find each angle of a regular polygon and use the sum to find a missing angle, on my own.
I can explain why a polygon's exterior angles always add to a full turn, no matter how many sides it has.
I can teach the angle sum rule and use it on a polygon nobody has counted the sides of for me.

skills.name: Complex numbers
levels: I have seen a number written with i, the square root of negative one, in it.
With a hint I can add, subtract or multiply two complex numbers.
I can multiply by a conjugate and solve a quadratic with complex roots on my own.
I can explain why every quadratic has two roots once complex numbers are allowed.
I can teach complex numbers and use them in a problem that hides them at first.

skills.name: Logarithms
levels: I have seen a logarithm written as the power that gets you to a number.
With a hint I can evaluate a simple logarithm or apply one property.
I can use log properties and change of base to evaluate a logarithm exactly, on my own.
I can explain why a logarithm and an exponential undo each other.
I can teach logarithms and use them to solve an equation with the variable in the exponent.

skills.name: Matrices
levels: I have seen numbers arranged in rows and columns used to hold a system of equations.
With a hint I can add two matrices or multiply one by a number.
I can multiply matrices, find a determinant, and invert a 2 by 2 matrix on my own.
I can explain why a matrix times its inverse gives the identity matrix.
I can teach matrices and use one to solve a system I have not seen.

skills.name: Vectors
levels: I have seen an arrow with both a length and a direction used to show a push or a move.
With a hint I can add two vectors or scale one by a number.
I can find a vector's magnitude and use the dot product to find an angle, on my own.
I can explain why the dot product is zero when two vectors are perpendicular.
I can teach vectors and use them in a problem about a force or a direction.

skills.name: Sequences
levels: I have seen a list of numbers that follows a rule from one term to the next.
With a hint I can find the next term of an arithmetic or geometric sequence.
I can write a sequence explicitly or recursively and find any term on my own.
I can explain why an arithmetic sequence adds the same amount and a geometric one multiplies.
I can teach sequences and find the rule behind a pattern I have not seen.

skills.name: Series
levels: I have seen a long sum of a sequence's terms written with a sigma sign.
With a hint I can add up a short arithmetic or geometric series.
I can find an arithmetic, geometric or infinite geometric sum on my own.
I can explain why an infinite geometric series only settles on a sum when the ratio is small enough.
I can teach series and spot a telescoping sum that collapses to a few terms.

skills.name: Conic sections
levels: I have seen a parabola, ellipse, or hyperbola come from slicing a cone or from an equation.
With a hint I can match an equation to a parabola, ellipse, or hyperbola.
I can derive a parabola from its focus and directrix and read an ellipse or hyperbola from its equation, on my own.
I can explain why a circle is a special case of an ellipse with equal axes.
I can teach conic sections and recognize one from an equation I have not seen.

skills.name: Trig functions
levels: I have seen sine, cosine and tangent defined for any angle around the unit circle.
With a hint I can find the exact value of sine or cosine at a special angle.
I can graph sine, cosine or tangent and read its amplitude, period and phase shift, on my own.
I can explain why the unit circle gives the same values the right triangle ratios give.
I can teach trig functions and read one off a graph or a radian measure I have not seen.

skills.name: Trig identities
levels: I have seen one trig expression rewritten as an equal one using an identity.
With a hint I can apply the Pythagorean identity to simplify an expression.
I can use the sum, difference or double angle identities to prove an identity on my own.
I can explain why proving an identity means showing both sides are the same function.
I can teach trig identities and pick the right one to simplify an expression I have not seen.

skills.name: Polar and parametric
levels: I have seen a point located by a distance and an angle instead of by x and y.
With a hint I can convert one point between polar and rectangular coordinates.
I can convert equations between the two systems and eliminate the parameter from a parametric equation, on my own.
I can explain why eliminating the parameter turns two equations for x and y into one relation.
I can teach polar and parametric equations and choose the easier system for a curve I have not seen.

skills.name: Limits
levels: I have seen a limit as the height a graph approaches as x gets close to a point.
With a hint I can read a limit from a graph or a table.
I can evaluate a limit algebraically and tell when it fails to exist, on my own.
I can explain why a limit can exist even where the function itself is undefined.
I can teach limits and find one at infinity or across an asymptote I have not seen.

skills.name: The derivative
levels: I have seen a derivative as the slope of a curve at a single point.
With a hint I can build a difference quotient and take its limit.
I can find a derivative from its limit definition and read one off a graph, on my own.
I can explain why a function must be continuous to be differentiable.
I can teach the derivative and build a tangent line for a curve I have not seen.

skills.name: Differentiation rules
levels: I have seen a shortcut that finds a derivative without the limit definition.
With a hint I can apply the power rule to a polynomial.
I can differentiate a product, a quotient and a composed function on my own.
I can explain why the chain rule multiplies an inner rate by an outer one.
I can teach the differentiation rules and combine several on a function I have not seen.

skills.name: Applications of the derivative
levels: I have seen a derivative used to find where a curve turns or a rate is changing.
With a hint I can find a critical point and test whether it is a max or a min.
I can solve a related rates or an optimization problem with derivatives on my own.
I can explain why the second derivative's sign tells concavity, not direction.
I can teach these applications and sketch a full curve I have not seen from its derivatives.

skills.name: Integrals
levels: I have seen an area under a curve built from thin rectangles.
With a hint I can approximate an area with a Riemann sum.
I can evaluate a definite integral with the fundamental theorem on my own.
I can explain why the fundamental theorem links an area to a derivative.
I can teach integrals and find an accumulation function I have not seen.

skills.name: Integration techniques
levels: I have seen an integral solved by undoing the chain rule with a substitution.
With a hint I can pick a u for a substitution and rewrite the integral.
I can integrate with substitution and use it to find an area or a volume, on my own.
I can explain why the bounds of a definite integral change with a substitution.
I can teach these techniques and set up a volume of revolution I have not seen.

skills.name: Differential equations
levels: I have seen an equation that relates a rate of change to the quantity itself.
With a hint I can separate the variables in a simple differential equation.
I can solve a separable equation and model exponential growth or decay on my own.
I can explain why a slope field shows every solution without solving the equation.
I can teach differential equations and read a slope field I have not seen.

skills.name: Recursion
levels: I have seen a sequence defined by its own earlier terms, like the Euclidean algorithm.
With a hint I can compute a few terms of a recursive rule.
I can write a recursion for a count and find its closed form on my own.
I can explain why a recursive rule and its closed form always agree.
I can teach recursion and prove a count is right for a rule I have not seen.
